content: JP-8, also known as Jet Propellant 8, is a kerosene-based jet fuel widely used by the United States military. It is specified under MIL-DTL-83133 and British Defence Standard 91-87, and it closely resembles the commercial aviation fuel Jet-A. JP-8 was first introduced at NATO bases in 1978 and is expected to remain in use at least until 2025. Its NATO code is F-34. The U.S. Air Force transitioned completely from JP-4 to JP-8 by the fall of 1996 to enhance safety and combat survivability, as JP-8 is less flammable and less hazardous. The U.S. Navy, on the other hand, uses JP-5, a similar fuel with an even higher flash point of over 60°C (140°F), though its higher cost restricts its use to aircraft carriers and other high-risk fire environments. JP-8 has been adopted as a replacement for diesel fuel in nearly all tactical ground vehicles and electrical generators used by the U.S. military. It is also employed as a coolant in engines and certain aircraft components. The use of a single fuel type simplifies logistics significantly. JP-8 is formulated with additives such as icing inhibitors, corrosion inhibitors, lubricants, and antistatic agents. Compared to JP-4, it contains lower levels of benzene, a known carcinogen, and n-hexane, a neurotoxin. However, JP-8 has a stronger odor than JP-4 and feels oily to the touch, whereas JP-4 has a solvent-like texture. When used in highly supercharged diesel engines with low compression ratios (approximately 14:1 or lower), JP-8 can cause issues during cold starts and idling. This is due to low compression temperatures and ignition delays, as the cetane index is not specified to be 40 or higher in MIL-DTL-83133G. Additionally, the lack of a specified lubricity standard under the BOCLE method in MIL-DTL-83133G can lead to wear problems in high-pressure fuel pumps and injectors in modern common rail diesel engines. Another issue in diesel engines is increased wear on outlet valve seats in cylinder heads, as the standard does not specify a minimum sulfur content. Sulfur in fuels typically contributes to the formation of damping soot layers on valve seats, which helps reduce wear. The standard notes that a cetane index value may be included in future revisions. Workers exposed to JP-8 have reported experiencing its smell and taste for hours after contact. Because JP-8 is less volatile, it remains on contaminated surfaces for longer periods, increasing the risk of exposure. A variant of JP-8, known as JP-8+100 (NATO code F-37), includes an additive that enhances its thermal stability by 56°C (100°F). This additive, introduced in 1994, is a combination of a surfactant, metal deactivator, and antioxidant. It was developed to reduce choking and fouling in engine fuel systems. Commercially, this additive is used in Boeing aircraft operated by KLM and in police helicopters in Tampa, Florida. JP-8+100 is also utilized by the Canadian Forces in CP-140 Aurora and CC-130 Hercules aircraft.
